fields.h1: Build a Dental Patient Survey Your Office Acts On
fields.hero_description: Build a dental patient survey patients answer on a phone after each visit, with low scores sent to your office manager.
fields.features_heading: What the Survey Asks and Who Sees Each Answer
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the survey, the alerts, and the results page from your prompt, and a follow-up prompt changes any of them.
fields.feature_1:
Questions about the visit, not the chart

List what the practice wants to hear about: booking, the wait, the front desk, and the cost. Emergent drafts a question for each, and you change any of them with a prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Sent the evening of the appointment

Connect your scheduling software through its API, and the app emails each patient the survey link on the evening of the visit, while the wait and the checkout are still fresh.
fields.feature_3:
Low scores reach one named person

Pick the score that needs a reply, such as a 1 or 2 on the wait. The app emails that answer and its comment to the office manager, with the patient's name and phone number.
fields.feature_4:
Results split by office and provider

Ask which office the patient visited and who they saw, and every chart can split on either one. A group with three offices compares them question by question on one page.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen on a phone

Patients answer one question per screen on their phone, with large buttons for each score. There is no cap on responses, whether 40 patients answer in a month or 4,000 do.
fields.feature_6:
Answers and code the practice keeps

Every answer is a row in a database the practice owns, tagged with the date and the office. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep changing it.

fields.usecase_heading: What Four Practices Learned From Patients
fields.tab_content_1:
Monday mornings, home to 8 of 11 low wait scores

Winnow Creek Family Dental emails a 5-question survey the evening of every cleaning. Any wait score of 1 or 2 emails office manager Ines Haverty the comment. In September, 11 of 248 patients rated the wait that low, and 8 of those 11 had a Monday morning slot. She added a second hygienist on Monday mornings.
fields.tab_content_2:
23 of 96 parents unsure of the next visit

Sprout Lane Pediatric Dentistry asks the parent 4 questions after each visit, then hands the phone to the child for a last screen of faces. In October, 81 of 96 children tapped the smile. On the parent side, 23 of 96 said they did not know what the next visit would involve. Every visit summary now ends with one line about it.
fields.tab_content_3:
After-school times ranked first by 58 families

Kestrel Orthodontics sends families one survey 6 months into treatment. Its main question asks them to rank 4 changes that would make visits easier: after-school times, shorter waits, text reminders, and parking. Of 140 families, 58 ranked after-school times first. The practice now stays open on Thursdays until 7 pm.
fields.tab_content_4:
Sallow Hill trails its sister offices on explaining cost

Bellhaven Dental Group runs one survey across its 3 offices and asks every patient whether someone went over the cost before they paid. At Cedar Gate, 112 of 123 patients said yes, and at Orchard Row, 95 of 108. Sallow Hill trailed with 57 of 89. Its front desk now reviews the estimate at checkout.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Dental Patient Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a dental patient survey that asks about the visit and puts each low score in front of someone who can fix it.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List what the practice will change
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask about the visit, not the treatment
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Use one scale for every rating
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set how often patients get it
fields.howto_step_1_des: Before you write a question, list the decisions the answers could change: opening hours, front desk staffing, how costs get explained. A question that cannot change anything comes out. Put that list in your prompt, and Emergent drafts the survey around it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Keep every question on what the patient saw and heard outside the treatment itself, like the waiting room and checkout. Questions about symptoms or care decisions belong in the chair with the dentist, not in a survey the office manager reads at the end of the week.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Rate each question on the same 1 to 5 scale, with 1 as poor and 5 as excellent. One scale lets you compare questions with each other and this month with last month. End with one open question about the single thing the office could do better.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose between a survey after every visit and one per patient each quarter. A family that comes in four times a year should not answer the same questions four times. Put the rule in your prompt, and the app applies it before each email goes out.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Give each low score an owner
fields.howto_step_5_des: Pick one person per kind of low score: the office manager for the wait, the billing coordinator for cost. Set the score that triggers an email to them, 2 or lower for example, and agree that the patient hears back within 2 business days.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send the survey to two staff members before any patient sees it. Time how long it takes on a phone, check that a test score of 1 reaches the right inbox, and rewrite any question that someone had to read twice.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once a quarter, name one change the answers led to, in the waiting room and in the next survey email. Say what the patients asked for and the month the change starts, such as a later evening slot or a new step at checkout.

faq_plan.q: What is a dental patient survey?
faq_plan.a: A dental patient survey is a short set of questions a dental practice sends patients about their visit, such as how easy it was to book, how long they waited, and whether the cost was clear before they paid. The practice uses the answers to change how visits run, not to assess anyone's teeth.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a dental patient survey?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in a prompt to Emergent's AI survey builder: the questions, the rating scale, who gets an email when a score is low, and how the results should split. Emergent builds the survey, its database, and a results page, and you change any part of it with another prompt. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: What questions should a dental patient survey ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask about the parts of the visit the office controls. Cover how easy it was to get an appointment, whether the patient was seen on time, and how the front desk treated them. Then ask whether someone explained the cost before they paid and whether they would recommend the practice. Close with one open question about what the office should fix first.

faq_plan.q: What is the best time to send a dental patient survey?
faq_plan.a: Send it the same day, a few hours after the appointment ends, while the visit is still fresh. The timing logic matches a post purchase survey: ask soon after the experience, not a week later. One reminder 2 days later is plenty for a survey this short.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a dental patient survey have?
faq_plan.a: Keep a survey sent after every visit to 5 to 8 questions: one each for scheduling, waiting, the staff, and cost, a recommend question, and one open question. Save a longer survey for once a year. Emergent builds it with one question per screen, and a patient answers each with one tap on a phone.

faq_plan.q: Should a dental patient survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Not fully: make the name field optional. A named answer lets the office manager call the patient back, while an anonymous one may draw blunter comments with no way to follow up. With an optional field, patients who want a call leave a name, and the rest can still answer.

faq_plan.q: How can a dental patient survey show which changes patients want most?
faq_plan.a: Ask patients to rank a short list of possible changes, such as later hours, shorter waits, or easier parking, instead of rating each one. A ranking survey forces a choice. The change put first most often is the one to start with. Keep the list to 4 or 5 options, and add a comment box for anything you did not list.

faq_plan.q: Can a dental patient survey ask only happy patients for online reviews?
faq_plan.a: Not for Google reviews. Its contributor policy lists things merchants may not do, including to "selectively solicit positive reviews from customers." If your survey links to a review page, show that link whatever score the patient gave. Handle the follow-up on low scores as a separate step.

faq_plan.q: What should the office do when a dental patient survey comes back with a low score?
faq_plan.a: Call the patient and ask what happened before explaining anything. Note what the office promised. Then check the month's scores for a pattern: several low wait scores on one weekday point to the schedule rather than one bad visit. In a survey Emergent builds, every response is stored in a database you own, and a prompt can add a call notes field beside each one.

faq_plan.q: How do you run a dental patient survey for children?
faq_plan.a: Ask the parent the questions and give the child one screen of their own, such as three faces to tap. Ask the child only how the visit felt, in words a 5-year-old knows. A list of funny survey questions can supply an icebreaker, but keep the rating questions plain so answers compare. Emergent builds the face scale from a one-line prompt.

plan.angle: The ranking pages are dental survey templates: a fixed list of 6 to 13 questions about booking, the front desk, cleanliness and an overall rating, and they stop there. This page shows four dental practices running their own survey with real numbers: a family practice that alerts its office manager on low wait scores, a pediatric office where parents answer and the child taps a face, an orthodontist asking families to rank what would make visits easier, and a three-office group comparing whether patients heard their cost before paying. The FAQ covers the questions to ask, timing, length, anonymity, ranking priorities, online reviews, low scores and surveying children; the how-to covers what to ask about the visit and who acts on each answer. It stays on the visit itself and gives no clinical advice.
